In English, the name of one person, as t.why: Held as a usage pattern seen hundreds of thousands of times per name ('Harry is' alone 549,335 times in Dolma) and as the textbook rule that a verb agrees with its subject. It could also be derived (a name of one person is singular; a singular subject takes a singular verb), but the pattern is so frequent that it is rated stored (unlikely) and no premises are listed. Plural forms are not counted bare: 'Harry are' is dominated by coordinations ('Neville and Harry are'). The fixed phrases of queries 3 and 4 are counted against their plural-verb versions.

notes: Mirrors grammar-replace-0005: the original rule is removed. New members reach the answer only through it (does not know). A fixed phrase stored whole keeps its form (nothing needs to give way under a delete); one built from the rule loses it. The user's agreement edit ('Harry is good' to 'Harry are good'), made a rule about the class 'name of one person' so that it is a TBox edit; it covers the whole verb (is/are, has/have, wants/want). Restricted to ordinary present-tense statements: the past subjunctive 'if Harry were here' and the mandative 'that Harry be' are correct today and kept out of every prompt (the review's R1 trap). Coordinations ('Harry and Sally are') are not names of one person. Determinate queries use names invented for the prompt (Zorvan, Melvara), so the rule is the only route; their prompts avoid the frame 'Zorvan is' so they do not contain their answer. World structure (coordinator's rule, README Decisions 2): in a world where a fixed phrase is stored whole, the phrase's class membership gives way and it falls under a wider, unedited rule that still gives the original form; it never stands as an exception to the edited rule, which would be the inconsistent patch. The two phrases are independent storage choices, so four worlds. The edited rule sits inside a wider unedited rule and overrides it for its class, as specific rules do in English ('children' overrides plural '-s'). Under delete, the wider rule would re-derive the deleted one, so the delete record's worlds also cut the class's link to it (README, Delete under determinacy: a derived fact's delete makes a premise go; the wider rule cannot go, being anchored by countless instances outside the chain). 'Big Brother' and 'Uncle Sam' are chosen because their membership can really give way: each is a personification (of the Party, of the US government) that can be read as a title rather than a person's name, and a singular noun phrase that is not a person's name still takes a singular verb. 'Santa Claus is coming to town' was considered and dropped: there is no natural reading of 'Santa Claus' as anything but one person, so its stored world would be a patch. The group reading of 'Harry' (a band name, 'Coldplay are') is not used (British collective-agreement R1 fuzz). Agreement compares the verb's number with the subject's: fol. Forced-choice questions throughout.
